title: Financial Mathematics 1: Earning Money

findings.finding: Vary Alison's output across the threshold while keeping both payment rates fixed.
findings.breakdown: The sequence exposes that only arrangements above 20 receive the higher rate.
findings.checked: The existing scaffold establishes payment for the first 20 plus payment for the excess. The proposed answers follow that model and use methods available here.
findings.assumptions: Use the sliding-scale interpretation explicitly established by p24-q9-a's scaffold.

repair.proposal: Immediately after p24-q9-a, add: 'Predict how earnings will change before calculating.' Under Alison's existing payment conditions, add further parts asking for earnings from (i) 19 arrangements [$129.20], (ii) 20 [$136.00], (iii) 21 [$144.90], and (iv) 22 [$153.80]. Follow with (v) 26 arrangements [$189.40]. Only output varies; the threshold and both rates remain fixed.

findings.doneWhen: The further parts compare earnings immediately below, at and above the threshold, followed by an unpatterned calculation.

findings.finding: The examples use percentage conversion, substitution with multiplication before addition, and decimal-coefficient equations without an opening review of these prerequisites.
findings.breakdown: Taylor requires division by a decimal coefficient; Aspen requires subtracting the retainer before dividing. Charles also requires evaluating a substituted sum and product in the correct order.
findings.checked: The complete earlier teaching supplies financial multiplication and division, but the immediately preceding piecework topic does not rehearse these percentage and equation forms. p25-method and p26-method give financial solution instructions rather than prerequisite review questions.
findings.assumptions: These are prior skills consistent with the course library. Calculators are assumed; the concern is setting up operations and equations.

repair.proposal: Before p25-royalties-information, add: (a) Write 6%, 0.4% and 1.25% as decimals. [0.06, 0.004, 0.0125] (b) Evaluate P = 300 + 0.04S when S = 8000. [620] (c) Solve 900 = 0.06x. [15000] (d) Solve 1400 = 200 + 0.03x. [40000] Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The review rehearses percentage conversion, substitution and the equation forms used by the examples.

findings.finding: Follow the equal-pay calculation with comparisons on either side of the crossover.
findings.breakdown: Students connect the $40000 crossover to which payment option earns more.
findings.checked: At $30000, the options pay $1200 and $1050. At $50000, they pay $1600 and $1750. Both calculations use the taught retainer-plus-commission method.
findings.assumptions: Both options use the same weekly sales value.

repair.proposal: Treat the existing question as part (a). Add (b) 'By how much does option 1's pay exceed option 2's pay when William sells $30000 in a week?' [$150] (c) 'By how much does option 2's pay exceed option 1's pay when William sells $50000 in a week?' [$150]

findings.doneWhen: Students compare the options below and above the equal-pay sales figure.

findings.finding: The salary examples use the year-to-fortnight and year-to-week relationships without an opening review.
findings.breakdown: Students must select 26 as the divisor and 52 as the multiplier. These relationships were taught before several intervening topics.
findings.checked: p3-teaching establishes both relationships. The immediately preceding royalties and commissions topic does not rehearse them. p31-salary supplies the fortnightly factor but contains no retrieval question. Monthly conversion is excluded from the claimed missing pieces because neither worked example uses it.
findings.assumptions: Calculators are assumed; selecting conversion factors is the prerequisite being reviewed.

repair.proposal: Before p31-salary, add: (a) Complete: 1 year = ___ weeks. [52] (b) Complete: 1 year = ___ fortnights. [26] (c) Convert $52000 per year to fortnightly pay. [$2000] (d) Convert $900 per week to annual pay. [$46800] Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse both time factors and their use before the salary examples.

findings.finding: The bonuses and allowances examples depend on percentage-of-quantity and hourly-wage calculations without an opening review.
findings.breakdown: Renee requires finding a percentage of salary. Vicki requires converting daily working hours into weekly hours and calculating normal wages before adding an allowance.
findings.checked: These methods appear in royalties and commissions and wages. Neither is rehearsed by the immediately preceding salary teaching; its examples convert pay periods.
findings.assumptions: Calculators are assumed. The review concerns choosing and setting up the calculations.

repair.proposal: Before p38-definitions, add: (a) Find 6% of $42000. [$2520] (b) Find 3% of $58000. [$1740] (c) Calculate weekly wages at $24.50 per hour for 30 hours. [$735] (d) Calculate weekly wages at $26.40 per hour for 4 hours a day over 5 days. [$528] Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Percentage and wage calculations are rehearsed before the examples combine them with extra payments.

findings.finding: Jeremy's complete numerical bonus task is repeated without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: Both copies give Jeremy a 3% bonus on $43600 and request total annual pay. The later completion scaffold repeats the same calculation.
findings.checked: Compared both complete tasks: person, salary, percentage and requested quantity are unchanged. The scaffold introduces no additional mathematical task, and no instructional purpose for the repeated values is stated.
findings.assumptions: Both tasks are completed in booklet order.

repair.proposal: Keep p38-a. Change p39-q4 to: 'Jeremy receives a bonus of 4% of his annual salary of $46800. Calculate his total pay for the year.' Retain its scaffold with Bonus = 4% of $46800 = $1872; Total annual pay = $46800 + $1872 = $48672.

findings.doneWhen: The later copy retains its structure and scaffold with different values and consistent answers.

findings.finding: The first unknown-rate question combines an overall tax percentage with reversal of the bracket formula and conversion to cents per dollar.
findings.breakdown: Students must first recognise that 25.8% determines total tax, then isolate the tax on the excess and recover a different rate. Treating 25.8% as the bracket rate gives the wrong calculation.
findings.checked: The full preceding exercise builds forward tax calculations and cumulative base taxes, but supplies no intermediate question linking an overall percentage to an unknown marginal rate. Earlier decimal-equation teaching supplies the algebra, not this connection. The question is followed by another reverse-rate task, so it is not merely the exercise's closing challenge.
findings.assumptions: Calculators and prior elementary equation solving are assumed.

repair.proposal: Add: 'First calculate 25.8% of $90000 to find the total tax. Subtract the base tax to find the tax on the income above $78800, then use this excess to find the rate in cents per dollar.'

findings.doneWhen: The question provides a route from the overall percentage to the unknown bracket rate while leaving students to perform the calculations.

findings.finding: Question 15's third-bracket base contradicts the cumulative-base relationship explicitly taught immediately beforehand.
findings.breakdown: The preceding bracket accumulates 0.22 × (54000 − 21000) = $7260, but the next bracket begins with $11880. This presents an inconsistent model of how base tax is formed.
findings.checked: p56-q12 explicitly defines base tax as accumulated tax from preceding brackets. Recalculation gives a third-bracket base of $7260 and a fourth-bracket base of $19970. Reducing part (b)'s tax by $4620 preserves its recovered rate of 41.9875 cents, rounded to 42 cents.
findings.assumptions: The fictional table follows the cumulative progressive-tax model taught in this topic.

repair.proposal: Change the third-bracket base from $11880 to $7260. In part (a), ask students to show x = $19970. In part (b), change tax payable to $31726.50. Answers: x = 7260 + 0.31(95000 − 54000) = $19970; y = (31726.50 − 19970) ÷ 28000 × 100 = 41.9875 cents, rounding to 42 cents.

findings.doneWhen: Every base equals the tax accumulated through preceding brackets, and both parts use the corrected values.

findings.finding: Compare equal income increments across the $45000 bracket boundary.
findings.breakdown: The run exposes that the tax increase changes at the boundary while tax itself remains continuous.
findings.checked: All proposed taxes agree with the supplied historical table. p51 addresses crossing a bracket, but the supplied practice has no equivalent run of equal income increments.

repair.proposal: After p52-q2-b, under the existing instruction, add: 'Predict how much tax will increase between consecutive incomes.' Add further parts with taxable incomes $43000 [$4712], $44000 [$4902], $45000 [$5092], $46000 [$5417], and $47000 [$5742]. Follow with the unpatterned income $62400 [$10747]. The table stays fixed while income increases by $1000 through the run.

findings.doneWhen: The further parts expose the change from $190 to $325 extra tax per $1000 of income.

findings.finding: The PAYG example combines tax-table calculation, pay-period conversion and net-income calculation without an opening review.
findings.breakdown: Following Charlie requires selecting and applying a tax-table row, converting annual amounts to fortnightly amounts and subtracting tax from gross pay.
findings.checked: Income tax immediately precedes PAYG, but the worked example combines that method with earlier salary conversion and net-income calculation. The standard's combined-method exception therefore applies. p58-payg-method restates the sequence without retrieval questions.
findings.assumptions: Calculators are assumed. Review uses the supplied historical tax table.

repair.proposal: Before p58-payg-method, add: (a) For taxable income $60000, state the bracket's base tax, decimal rate and excess. [$5092; 0.325; $15000] (b) Calculate annual tax on $60000. [$9967] (c) Convert $52000 annual salary to fortnightly pay. [$2000] (d) Gross annual income is $60000 and annual tax is $9967. Find annual net income. [$50033] Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse each earlier method that Charlie's example combines.

findings.finding: The integrated refund example combines taxable-income and progressive-tax calculations without an opening review of those earlier methods.
findings.breakdown: Sarah's example requires aggregating income, subtracting allowable deductions and selecting and applying the appropriate tax-table row before calculating the refund.
findings.checked: Both methods are taught earlier and combined in income-tax practice. They are not rehearsed in the immediately preceding PAYG topic as a complete pair. p60 rehearses refund balances, so that component is excluded. The combined-method review exception supports rehearsing the two remaining methods.
findings.assumptions: Calculators are assumed. Review uses the supplied historical table.

repair.proposal: At the topic opening, add: (1) A worker earns $32000 in wages and $500 interest, with $700 allowable deductions. Find taxable income. [$31800] (2) For taxable income $34000, state the previous bracket's upper limit, base tax and decimal rate. [$18200; $0; 0.19] (3) Calculate tax on $34000. [$3002] (4) Calculate tax on $60000. [$9967] Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students retrieve taxable-income calculation and tax-table application before the integrated example.

findings.finding: Joy's integrated example combines progressive-tax calculation and refund/liability interpretation without an opening review.
findings.breakdown: Students must retrieve tax-table selection and calculation, then interpret instalments minus total tax while incorporating the new levy.
findings.checked: Both methods are taught earlier. Although refund calculations occur in the preceding topic, the combined-method exception applies to Joy's integrated example. p65-practice rehearses taxable income and the new levy, but neither identified missing review component.
findings.assumptions: Calculators are assumed. Use the supplied historical tax table and the booklet's levy model.

repair.proposal: Before p65-introduction, add: (a) For taxable income $34000, state the base tax, decimal rate and excess, then calculate income tax. [$0; 0.19; $15800; $3002] (b) Repeat for $76000. [$5092; 0.325; $31000; $15167] (c) Tax payable is $6200 and instalments total $5700. Calculate instalments minus tax and state the outcome. [−$500; $500 owing] (d) Repeat for tax payable $4800 and instalments $5150. [$350; $350 refund] Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse tax-table calculations and both signs of the refund/liability balance before the combined example.

findings.finding: Recalculate Catriona's total tax and refund after one additional allowable deduction.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects a deduction to reductions in both income tax and the Medicare levy.
findings.checked: The additional $100 deduction lowers rounded taxable income from $86124 to $86024. Income tax becomes $18424.80 and the levy $1720.48, giving total tax $20145.28. Instalments remain $26156, so the refund becomes $6010.72, an increase of $34.50.
findings.assumptions: Use the original question's historical table, levy model and rounding instructions.

repair.proposal: After p70-q10-e, add: (f) 'Catriona discovers another $100 allowable deduction. What is her revised total tax payable?' [$20145.28] (g) 'What is her revised tax refund?' [$6010.72] (h) 'By how much has her refund increased?' [$34.50]

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up links one additional deduction to both tax components and the resulting refund.

contextQuestions.question: Have students already learned that profit equals revenue minus costs, including the meaning of revenue? The supplied teaching does not establish this, and the course-library titles do not resolve it. If it is new, Shirley's question needs that short teaching cue.

protectedGroups.observation: Converting the same duration back reverses multiplication into division.
protectedGroups.invariant: The duration and the factor of 12 between years and months.

protectedGroups.observation: The route through years works in both directions between months and weeks.
protectedGroups.varies: Conversion direction and the order of the factors.
protectedGroups.invariant: The equivalent duration under the 52-week convention.

protectedGroups.observation: At a fixed hourly rate, earnings scale with hours.
With the same weekly hours, changing the hourly rate changes weekly earnings.
protectedGroups.varies: Hourly rate and the amount of supplied working.
protectedGroups.invariant: 7 hours per day and 5 days per week.

protectedGroups.observation: Hourly wages exclude a separately received tip; students first have a visual decomposition and then apply it independently.
protectedGroups.invariant: Subtract the tip from total receipts before dividing by hours.

protectedGroups.observation: Successive parts expose which pay bands apply as total hours cross the agreement's thresholds.
protectedGroups.invariant: The normal hourly rate and the 35-hour normal band followed by five time-and-a-half hours.

protectedGroups.observation: The same total earnings can correspond to different missing actual hours depending on the pay category.
protectedGroups.varies: The missing category: normal, time-and-a-half, then double time.
protectedGroups.invariant: $40 normal hourly rate, $1200 total pay and eight hours in each of the two given categories.

protectedGroups.observation: A retainer changes total pay without changing commission; changing the rate changes commission at fixed sales.
protectedGroups.varies: First the retainer changes from $0 to $1000, then the commission rate changes from 5% to 10%.
protectedGroups.invariant: Sales remain $10 000; each adjacent pair holds the other pay parameter fixed.

protectedGroups.observation: Additional sales activate successive commission bands while completed bands retain their contributions.
protectedGroups.varies: Sale price reaches the first boundary, then the second band, then the third band.
protectedGroups.invariant: The fixed payment, rates and band boundaries.

protectedGroups.observation: A fixed annual income produces different periodic payments according to the number of periods in a year.
protectedGroups.varies: Requested payment period: week, fortnight, month.
protectedGroups.invariant: Annual salary of $68600 and the annual-pay division method.

protectedGroups.observation: The same annual salary can be expressed consistently across three payment periods.
protectedGroups.varies: Requested payment period: week, fortnight, month.
protectedGroups.invariant: Annual salary of $74250 and the annual-pay division method.

protectedGroups.observation: All income sources and all allowable deductions must be included before applying the levy.
protectedGroups.varies: Whether income, deductions or both contain multiple amounts.
protectedGroups.invariant: Add incomes, subtract total deductions, then multiply taxable income by 0.02.
